1:
Jerusalem had to be repopulated by lot, and Henry begins by asking why that should have been necessary at all. The place is called the holy city because the temple stood there and God had chosen to put his name there; one would think the holy seed would have striven for a habitation in it. Instead they declined it, and Henry offers three reasons. A stricter manner of life was expected of those who lived there than of anyone else, and men who do not care to be holy themselves are shy of a holy city. It was also the place most hated by the surrounding nations, against which their designs were levelled — the post of danger, as the post of honour usually is — and the fear of trouble keeps many from appearing for God at all, forgetting that a city singled out for malice is also singled out for protection. And thirdly it was simply poorer: Jerusalem was no trading town, and money could be made in the country by corn and cattle that could not be made there.

Henry will not leave that third reason as a piece of economic description. Most people, he says, prefer their own wealth, credit, pleasure, ease and safety to the glory of God and the public good, and that is a general and just complaint rather than a fact about one generation.

The replenishing came about two ways, and the witnesses divide their attention between them. Gill and Henry both begin with the rulers. Gill gives the practical grounds — the capital was where their offices had to be discharged, where the city had to be defended, and where their example would encourage others to settle. Henry adds that the seats of judgment were there, so that difficult cases came up to them, and then makes the point that interests him most: the mighty are magnetic. When great men choose the holy city for their home, their example brings holiness into reputation and their zeal provokes many.

The second way was voluntary, and it is the one every witness praises. Gill distinguishes these men from those the lot had taken: they settled of their own accord, and the people wished them happiness because they had given up ease and profit for the common good. Clarke calls the offer a sacrifice to patriotism, the city affording few advantages and considerable danger. Wesley says the same in harder terms — Jerusalem was the butt of every malicious plot, and for the present it cost its inhabitants more than it brought them. Henry records what the volunteers were after: they sought the good of Jerusalem because of the house of the Lord their God, and that is why it stands to their honour that they moved when others hung back.

What the people did in return is described in one word, and the commentators unfold it. Gill and Clarke both take the blessing to include prayer for them; Henry divides it three ways — they praised the men, prayed for them, and praised God for them — and adds a dry observation, that many who will not put themselves forward for the public good will at least give a good word to those who do. Delitzsch, looking ahead to the register, notes that the province named in it is the land of Judah as a division of the Persian empire, and warns against reading a contrast into the repeated verb about dwelling, which is merely a pleonasm.
3:
A heading opens the register, and the word province carries more weight than it looks. Gill and Wesley both gloss it as Judea, reduced to a province by the king of Babylon and now held as one under Persia. Ellicott hears the writer's own position in the term: it betrays the hand of a man who was a Persian official as well as governor of Judah, and it marks this sentence as a general heading covering everything that follows — country as well as capital. He adds that Israel is used here as a generic name, the two remaining tribes standing for the whole, exactly as Judah had done earlier.

Clarke compares the list with the parallel register and finds a real difference of scope. That one numbers only those who returned with Zerubbabel; this one takes in those and the people who came up afterwards with Ezra and with Nehemiah. The two are therefore not rival versions of one census but counts taken at different depths of the same settlement.

The city itself straddled a tribal boundary, and Gill makes that the reason two tribes appear together in it: Jerusalem belonged partly to Judah and partly to Benjamin, and was inhabited by both, as it had been from the first. Delitzsch sorts the Judahite entries into two heads, one from the line of Perez and the other from the line of Shelah, and repeats a correction he has made elsewhere — that the form naming the second family is wrongly pointed and should be read as the Shelanite. He treats one of the names in the chain as a proper name rather than a description, and admits that neither head is known from anywhere else.

Gill works the second pedigree through its links — Baruch, Colhozeh, Hazaiah, Adaiah, Joiarib, Zechariah — back to a forefather he suspects is Shelah the son of Judah under another form, and identifies the head himself with a man named slightly differently in the parallel list. Delitzsch counts the result: four hundred and sixty-eight able men of the sons of Perez, which he understands as four hundred and sixty-eight heads of families rather than individuals.
6:
The Judahite total is given first, and Gill reads the description of the men as bearing on why they were wanted: four hundred and sixty-eight valiant men, well qualified to defend the city against its enemies. The register is a muster as much as a census.

Benjamin follows with the larger figure, and Gill notices it. There were more Benjamites than men of Judah in the city — perhaps because the tribe held a greater share of it, or perhaps because they were simply better disposed to live there. Ellicott counts two Benjamite families and observes that they supplied the city with both of its prefects.

How many men stand behind the second name is where Gill and Delitzsch part. Gill reads two — Gabbai and Sallai — following the head of the house. Delitzsch reads one, a single compound name, Gabbai-Sallai, and counts two heads of houses for Benjamin rather than three. The nine hundred and twenty-eight he takes, as he took the Judahite figure, for fathers of families.

The two officers named next are distinguished by rank rather than by tribe. Gill calls the first the chief governor of the city. Clarke makes him magistrate with the second man as his deputy, while allowing that the two may have held different offices rather than the same office at two levels. Wesley gives the first a military sense instead, as captain of their thousand.

With the priests the register turns over, and here the witnesses correct the text before reading it. Ellicott would have the opening names read as three, Jedaiah and Joiarib and Jachin, standing for three priestly families. Delitzsch agrees and explains how the error arose, the word for son having probably crept in before the second name through a copyist's slip; on his reading these are three heads of houses and so of priestly orders. He identifies the ruler of the house of God as a descendant of Ahitub, and puts the ministering priests of those three orders at eight hundred and twenty-two. Gill notes that the same account stands in the parallel chapter, with the one difference that the man called Seraiah here appears there as Azariah.
11:
The priestly section is a chain of names with numbers attached, and the witnesses concentrate on what the numbers describe. Delitzsch runs the pedigree of the ruler of the house of God back through Hilkiah and Zadok to Ahitub, then sets out the three totals the section gives — eight hundred and twenty-two, two hundred and forty-two, a hundred and twenty-eight — and names the overseer set above the last group. Gill explains what the largest figure covers: these were the men who did the work of the house, offering the sacrifices, burning the incense, setting on the shewbread, lighting the lamps. He identifies the second company as the kinsmen of the head just named.

The description attached to the third group is the one point of real disagreement, and it turns on whether the phrase is martial. Gill takes it both ways at once: they were able men for the work of their office as priests, and men of courage who could fight an enemy and defend the city if occasion arose. Clarke reads it as plainly military, marking them for strength of body and for courage in war. Ellicott refuses the martial sense altogether and glosses the words as ability for the service of God's house — men of capacity rather than of arms.

Delitzsch's way of counting matters here as it did earlier. The figures attached to each company are heads of families rather than individual men, so the priestly establishment the chapter describes is larger than its totals suggest at first reading, and the three groups are three orders rather than three bands of recruits. Gill's gloss on the largest of them points the same way: what they had in common was not a shared muster but a shared round of duties in the house.

Ellicott makes one further correction in the same breath. The phrase describing the overseer's father is not a description at all but a name, and should be read as son of Haggedolim rather than as son of one of the great men. Gill closes the passage by marking the transition, that the Levites named next are those who had their dwelling in the city.
16:
The Levitical offices are distinguished by what part of the house they touched. Delitzsch notes that the two men named first had oversight of the outward business of the house of God — the affairs that lay outside the sanctuary proper — and Gill sets them alongside the Levite named before them.

The next office is musical, and it draws the fullest comment. Delitzsch gives the man's function as the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer, with a second standing next to him among his brethren. Clarke translates the office into the vocabulary of his own day: the precentor, the pitcher of the tune, the master-singer. Wesley describes the occasion rather than the title. The public and solemn prayers and praises were constantly joined to the morning and the evening sacrifice; the singers were present at both, and praised God with a psalm or hymn which this man began. Gill adds a small point of identification, that one of the forefathers in the chain appears under a different form of his name in the parallel record.

Then the totals. Gill gives the Levites of the holy city as two hundred and eighty-four with their residence there, and the gatekeepers as a hundred and seventy-two. Ellicott stops on that second figure because the parallel register gives two hundred and twelve instead, and he offers a partial explanation rather than a complete one: the other list is confined to those who returned with Zerubbabel, whereas this one adds the men who came up later with Ezra. He does not claim the difference is fully accounted for, and points the reader to his own discussion of the parallel chapter.

What the two lists have in common is more striking than where they diverge. The same handful of gatekeeping families appears in both, the same names recur among the singers, and the offices themselves — outward business, the beginning of the thanksgiving, the keeping of the gates — are described in nearly the same terms across a gap of generations. The register is recording continuity, and the arithmetic is the only place where it wobbles.
20:
The register turns from the capital to everywhere else, and Henry seizes the moment for a point about balance. Jerusalem had to be replenished, but not so far as to drain the country behind it; the king himself is served by the field, and the field does little service if there are no hands to work it. So he warns against the quarrel that might easily follow — no strife, no envy, no contempt, no ill will between the people of the cities and the people of the villages, since both are needful, both useful, and neither can be spared. Gill states the fact the verse gives more briefly, that the rest of Israel, priests and Levites alike, lived outside the city, every man in his own inheritance. Henry treats the arrangement as deliberate rather than residual: the lot had taken a tenth into the capital, and the nine parts left in the country were not a remainder but the other half of a single settlement, which is why he thinks the two populations needed warning against despising one another.

The temple servants are the exception, and the reason is practical. Henry explains that the descendants of the Gibeonites were settled on Ophel, against the wall, because the servile work of the temple fell to them and they had to be near enough to be at hand. Gill describes the place as a high point or tower on the wall; Delitzsch identifies it more exactly as the southern slope of Mount Moriah and names the two chiefs set over these men. Wesley gives the same location and the same reason.

Whether that settlement counted as inside the city is a question Ellicott raises and leaves standing. The promontory could be reckoned within the walls or outside them depending which line of wall was taken as the boundary; here, he judges, it is treated as outside. Delitzsch meanwhile declines an identification another scholar had proposed between one of the two chiefs and a name in the earlier roll of returning families. The argument does not hold, he says: that a division of temple servants descended from a given man is no reason to suppose one of their chiefs was that man himself.
22:
The Levites were scattered through the country towns, and Henry notes what kept them a single body notwithstanding: they had an overseer resident in the capital, the superior of their order, to whom they applied for direction, who managed their affairs and took cognisance of their conduct. Gill describes the same officer as the man who saw to it that they did their work in ministering to the priests, and traces his descent back to Asaph. Clarke renders the title itself as the visitant or inspector.

Delitzsch reads the verse as repairing an omission earlier in the chapter. The phrase about the business of the house of God belongs to a particular Levitical division named some verses back, whose chief had not been given, while the chiefs of the other two divisions had been; the reason, he suggests, is that this division's head was over the singers, and the singers had not yet been mentioned at that point. So the name is supplied here instead. Henry adds a detail about how those singers were employed between services — some were set to look after the necessary repairs of the temple, being ingenious men with time on their hands.

Who the king was who provided for them is disputed, and the witnesses lean the same way without quite agreeing. Gill reports that some understand David and prefers the king of Persia. Clarke names the alternatives outright and judges the Persian the more probable, since the provision in question was a daily allowance. Delitzsch simply states what was commanded, a fixed portion for the singers due every day.

The chapter's last officer is the one who dealt with that king, and here the disagreement is about where he sat. Delitzsch holds that the phrase can scarcely describe a royal commissioner stationed in Jerusalem; it designates a man transacting the community's affairs at the king's own court. Clarke puts him in Judah instead, as the governor appointed over the Jewish nation in matters where the civil power touched Jewish concerns, and supposes he fixed and levied and received the tribute. Ellicott calls him the king's agent in the country business of the province, and Wesley describes the work as judging civil causes by the law of that kingdom — between man and man, and between the king and the people in matters of tribute or grievance. Ellicott adds one observation that looks backward rather than forward: this man's descent from Zerah makes the absence of Zerah from the tribal lists at the head of the chapter very remarkable, and suggests something has dropped out by accident.
25:
With the capital accounted for, the register changes its unit. Gill marks the transition simply, that what follows is a list of the country cities and villages and who lived in them. Delitzsch describes the change more precisely, and it is a change in what the writer thought worth recording: the heads of houses who lived outside Jerusalem are no longer enumerated at all, only the towns with the settlements attached to them, and even those are given summarily. Names of places replace names of men, and the reason is presumably that the country settlements were resumed possessions rather than fresh assignments: a man in the villages was living where his family had lived, so there was nothing to record about him beyond the town he was in.

Two small points of language occupy him. The particle that introduces the section is used here in a way peculiar to this passage, standing for a respect or reference to something, where another word would ordinarily do that work. And the term rendered villages means, properly, enclosures — so the picture is of a walled or hedged settlement attached to its town rather than of a scatter of houses.

What the list then does is trace a territory. Delitzsch follows the Judahite settlements through their sequence of names and arrives at the summary the passage itself gives, that they dwelt from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom. The register is not merely recording where families ended up; it is stating how much ground the tribe was holding again, which for a community recently returned from exile is a claim as much as a description.

Gill's contribution here is the smallest in the chapter and the most practical: he simply notes that the account of the inhabitants follows, and lets the place-names carry their own weight without pressing them for more than they say. Neither witness attempts to identify every site, and Delitzsch is explicit that the writer did not intend an exhaustive account — which is worth registering, since a reader who treats a summary list as a complete one will draw wrong conclusions from whatever he finds missing from it.
30:
The southern reach is summed up in a phrase, and Ellicott measures it: from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom is the extreme south to the extreme north of Judah, some fifty miles of country. That is the extent the returned tribe was occupying again, and it is given in one line where the towns themselves take several.

Benjamin's territory follows, and the first name in it produces a genuine disagreement about geography. Gill places Geba on the southern border of Benjamin and Michmash on the northern, so that the two names bracket the tribe's land. Delitzsch identifies Geba instead as the northern boundary of the kingdom of Judah, fixing it at a half-ruined village some three leagues north of Jerusalem, with Michmash — which he equates with a site still bearing a version of the name — rather more than an hour's walk north-east of it. Clarke adds a third possibility, that Geba is probably the same place as the Gibeah associated with Saul. Ellicott is concerned only with the construction, and would render the opening so that the Benjamites are said to have dwelt from Geba onward.

Gill works through the rest of the names with the instincts of a gazetteer. One he identifies with the town east of Bethel; one is the birthplace of Jeremiah; one was a city of the priests; one he distinguishes carefully from a like-named place in Naphtali; two he admits are mentioned nowhere else at all. Where he can place a site he does, and where he cannot he says so — which is the same honesty Clarke shows on two of the same names, calling them simply unknown. On one point the two differ: Gill identifies a town with a later fortified place lying in a plain, where Clarke leaves it unidentified.

Delitzsch closes the enumeration with the note about the Levites, and reads it as a statement of movement rather than of property. Divisions of Levites that had belonged to Judah under the older arrangements now came to Benjamin — that is, they were living among the Benjamites, and the sentence records a redistribution rather than a boundary.
35:
The last towns in the list have a building history attached to them. Clarke reports that the pair named here were raised by the sons of a man recorded elsewhere in the Benjamite genealogies, and suspects that the settlement called the valley of craftsmen was built in the valley that gave it the name — a trade quarter rather than a district that happened to acquire a nickname from the people who drifted into it.

Then the chapter ends with the Levites, and the sentence about them is brief enough that all three witnesses comment on its brevity. Gill takes the divisions to mean that the Levites were scattered about, some here and some there, through both tribes, and gives the reason he thinks governed the scattering: the better instruction of the people. On that reading the dispersal is not a failure to settle them properly but the whole point of settling them at all, since a teaching order gathered into one place teaches nobody.

Clarke reads the same clause as placing the Levites within the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and rejects the rendering of one ancient version which would give them half of each — not likely, he says. He then draws out what the arrangement implies about their support. A people whose hearts were now turned toward the Lord would make the best provision they could for the work of God and for everyone engaged in it; but that provision cannot have been very great, since the full service was not yet established and the Levites themselves were few.

Ellicott makes the same observation from the other side, and it explains the manner of the notice rather than excusing it: it was the fewness of the Levites in the country that warranted summarising them in a single line. A register that has spent whole verses on the townships of Benjamin disposes of a whole tribe in nine words, and the disproportion is itself information about how thin the restored ministry still was. Between them the three witnesses turn a throwaway clause into the chapter's quietest finding: the land had been repopulated more successfully than the temple had been staffed.
